clue.text: Writer, illustrator, top farceur and snooker player

parts.note: to top someone is to beat them, outdo them
Brian Rix was the British actor famous for Whitehall farces
a snooker player pots balls, so is one who pots

explanation.surface: A list of talents, as if one versatile person wrote, drew, starred in farce and played snooker.
explanation.walkthrough: Brian Rix was a British actor-manager famed for stage farces at London's Whitehall Theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The creator of Peter Rabbit both wrote and illustrated her children's books.

clue.text: European guy mounts Guardian's entrance

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounting means climbing, so the word for guy is read upwards

parts.note: a guy is a man
the Guardian's own setter speaks of the paper as 'ours'

explanation.surface: A European man climbs up to the doorway of the newspaper's office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrance' is not a doorway but the verb, stressed on the second syllable: to delight.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to charm or captivate them, a synonym.

clue.text: Daily crime perpetrated by 24s

definitions.meaning: the Financial Times, a London daily newspaper, is known by its initials with a definite article in front
rabbits steal vegetables from Mr McGregor's garden in the Potter stories

explanation.surface: A routine offence committed by rabbits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' reads as an adjective but is a noun, a newspaper: the Financial Times, split as THE FT.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Rabbit's raids on the vegetable garden amount to stealing, a crime.

clue.text: Leaflets in series that is withdrawn for a short time

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the letters for 'that is' are taken out and something else is put in their place

parts.note: taken as written
T is the short form of time

explanation.surface: Leaflets in a magazine series are pulled for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'withdrawn for' means one thing is taken out and another put in its place. I.e. is the standard abbreviation for 'that is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Inserts are loose leaflets slipped into magazines and newspapers.

clue.text: Elemental form is uppermost in poet's heart

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word for uppermost goes inside the heart of poet
the heart of a word is its middle, here the middle pair of letters of poet

parts.note: uppermost means top

explanation.surface: Something elemental lies at the very top of a poet's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elemental' suggests something basic, but here it means of a chemical element. 'heart' takes the middle of 'poet' and 'in' puts uppermost inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An isotope is one of the forms of a chemical element, differing in neutron count.

clue.text: US male's crazy about tiny margin for 1 12 character

indicators.note: the anagram goes around the word for a tiny margin
crazy suggests the letters of 'US male's' are deranged into a new order

parts.note: winning by a whisker is winning by a tiny margin

explanation.surface: An American man is mad about winning by a hair, for a children's book character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' rearranges US MALE'S into SAMUELS; 'about' puts it around WHISKER. Samuel Whiskers is the rat in a Beatrix Potter tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Whiskers is the rat who captures Tom Kitten in a Beatrix Potter story.

clue.text: Everyone in the Times drinks? They're incredible

indicators.note: the word for everyone sits inside the two Ts

parts.note: times as multiplication is T, so plural times gives two Ts
everyone means all
ales are drinks

explanation.surface: Everyone at the Times newspaper drinks, which readers find hard to believe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Times' looks like the newspaper but gives TT, a T for each time.
explanation.definitionFit: Exaggerated stories are hard to believe: incredible in the literal sense.

clue.text: English university invested in secure publisher

indicators.note: being invested in something is being placed inside it

parts.note: to secure something is to pin it

explanation.surface: An English university puts money into a safe publishing house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invested in' reads as finance but means placed inside: ENGU inside PIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Penguin is a well-known British publishing house of paperbacks.

clue.text: Ginger had pics Photoshopped as part of this work

definitions.text: Ginger had pics Photoshopped as part of this work

indicators.note: pictures that are Photoshopped are digitally altered, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone called Ginger had pictures digitally edited for this puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: editing pictures is part of designing the illustrated themed grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Visual layout work, including retouching images, is the craft of a designer of pages.

clue.text: Brave enormous halves switch sides

indicators.note: the two halves of the word for enormous change places

parts.note: mega means enormous

explanation.surface: Something brave and enormous whose two halves swap over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'halves switch sides' turns ME-GA into GA-ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Game as an adjective means willing and plucky, ready to have a go.

clue.text: Climbing with difficulty, get lost jewellery

parts.note: scram is a curt command meaning go away
bling is flashy jewellery

explanation.surface: While struggling up a slope, one loses one's jewellery.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrambling is clambering awkwardly using hands and feet.

clue.text: See 1
It's for picking fruit et cetera, occasionally netted

indicators.note: netted means caught inside, so the plum holds the picked letters

parts.note: a plum is a fruit

indicators.note: occasionally means taking only some letters, here every other one

explanation.surface: A tool for picking fruit and so on, sometimes caught in a net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picking' suggests harvesting fruit, but the picking is of guitar strings. 'occasionally' takes every other letter and 'netted' places them inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plectrum is used to pluck, or pick, guitar strings.

clue.text: Trunk's for governor protecting social centre

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: protecting means surrounding, so the boss goes around the picked letters

parts.note: a governor is a boss

indicators.note: the centre of social is its middle pair of letters

explanation.surface: A trunk is good for a governor guarding a social club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunk' suggests luggage or a tree, but it is an elephant's nose. 'centre' takes the middle two letters of 'social'; 'protecting' wraps the boss around them.
explanation.definitionFit: An elephant's trunk is its long nose, a proboscis.

clue.text: They give support thus, when they're eaten by 24s

parts.note: bras are supportive undergarments
sic is Latin for thus
as can mean when

explanation.surface: Supportive things that get eaten by rabbits, an odd image.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabbages and their kin are vegetables that rabbits raid in Mr McGregor's garden.

clue.text: Dull Black Country character of 1 12

definitions.meaning: Pigling ___ is a pig in a Potter tale

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a land is a country

explanation.surface: A dull figure from the industrial West Midlands in a children's book.
explanation.walkthrough: The Black Country is the industrial West Midlands of England; here split into Black, B, and Country, LAND. Pigling Bland is a Potter pig.
explanation.definitionFit: Bland means insipid and unexciting, a synonym for dull.

clue.text: Greens back US city, ousting Liberal

indicators.note: ousting means one letter is thrown out
back means the name of the city is read in reverse

parts.note: Dallas is a city in Texas

explanation.surface: Green party politicians support an American city, ejecting the Liberal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' gives SALLAD from DALLAS, and 'ousting' removes one L.
explanation.definitionFit: A salad is a dish of leafy vegetables, so 'greens' in a loose sense.

clue.text: A short way to get round hardwood supplier

indicators.note: to get round something is to encircle it, so the shortened way surrounds a letter
short means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a way is a street
H stands for hard, as on pencils; the word also serves in the definition

explanation.surface: A shortcut road bends round a tree yielding timber.
explanation.walkthrough: The H comes from 'hard' in 'hardwood' (H for hard, as on pencils), doing double duty inside the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ash is a tree whose tough wood is classed as hardwood.

clue.text: Idiot pays criminal for property of 6 23

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters are wrongly or crookedly arranged

explanation.surface: A fool pays a crook for a piece of real estate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'property' looks like real estate but means a quality: Samuel Whiskers is a fat rat.
explanation.definitionFit: Adiposity means fatness, a trait of the plump rat Samuel Whiskers.

clue.text: Picture four rivers, one flowing into another

parts.note: the Po is an Italian river and R is the abbreviation for river; these are the first two of the four

indicators.note: flowing into means one river is put inside the other

parts.note: the Tay is a Scottish river
R is the abbreviation for a river

explanation.surface: A landscape painting of four rivers where one joins another.
explanation.walkthrough: The four rivers are PO, R, R and TAY; 'flowing into' puts one R inside TAY to make TRAY.
explanation.definitionFit: To picture something is to depict or represent it, a synonym.

clue.text: 1 12 character ignores Iggy — stars do it

indicators.note: ignores means the named letters are left out

parts.note: Mrs Tiggy-Winkle is the hedgehog washerwoman of the Potter books
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Potter character snubs Iggy Pop, as celebrities do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stars' looks like celebrities snubbing someone, but means stars in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Stars twinkle: their light seems to flicker in the night sky.

clue.text: I'm surprised troops nearly block river

indicators.note: to block a river is to sit inside it

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Britain

indicators.note: nearly means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: troops make up an army

explanation.surface: Astonishingly, most of the army dams a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' drops the last letter of the word for troops, and 'block' sets the rest inside the Dee, a river in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation expresses mild astonishment, the same as saying one is surprised.

clue.text: See 6
Bane of 26, teacher's pet ultimately

parts.note: a rabbi is a Jewish teacher

indicators.note: ultimately means the final letter is taken

explanation.surface: Something hated by a character, the teacher's pet at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'teacher's pet' looks like a favoured pupil, but the 's links RABBI to the last letter of 'pet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Rabbit and his kin are the pests Mr McGregor hunts in his garden.

clue.text: Poet, painter and illustrator left to cook hogs

indicators.note: hogs means monopolises, keeps to itself, so it holds the other letter inside

parts.note: to bake is to cook

explanation.surface: An artist leaves to cook some pigs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hogs' looks like pigs but is the verb: BAKE holds L.
explanation.definitionFit: William Blake was a poet who also painted and illustrated his own books.

clue.text: Oddly, more mice busily gorge on rare 1 12 character

indicators.note: oddly means the odd-numbered letters are taken
busily suggests the letters bustle about into a new order

explanation.surface: Strangely, extra mice feast hard on a rare dish, like a gardener's nightmare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' takes M R M C from MORE MICE; 'busily' rearranges GORGE plus R into GREGOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr McGregor is the gardener who chases Peter Rabbit in the Potter stories.

clue.text: A country's seabirds

parts.note: UK is a country, and the 's adds an S

explanation.surface: A nation's seabirds.
explanation.definitionFit: Auks are diving seabirds such as puffins and guillemots.

clue.text: Spots wine, then loses it

parts.note: to spot is to see
red is a wine

explanation.surface: Someone notices wine, then loses their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' looks like stains from spilt wine but is the verb: notices.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose it is to lose one's temper, become furious.

clue.text: Prepare to print 50-peseta curtains

indicators.note: curtains conceal what is behind them, so the answer is hidden in the words

parts.note: 50 is written out as the word fifty, joined to peseta, the old Spanish currency

explanation.surface: Preparing to print a curtain price tag in old Spanish money.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 50 as the word fifty: the answer sits concealed in fifTY-PESETa, as behind curtains, once the outer letters FIF and A are set aside. The pesetas were Spain's money before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: To typeset text is to arrange it in type ready for printing.
